B2B software is fragmenting. The cost barrier that forced buyers into generic tools is collapsing, and AI is what breaks it.

## Most B2B Software Is Generic by Necessity

For most of the last 20 years, the SaaS model worked like this: build once, sell to many. The economics required it. Custom software was expensive. The more a vendor could standardize their product, the more customers they could serve without proportionally growing their engineering team.

That constraint shaped everything. Most B2B buyers learned to accept software that almost fit. They hired consultants to bridge the gap. They built spreadsheets to handle edge cases. They paid for features they didn't use and worked around the ones they needed.

## A Framework for Thinking About It

Two axes matter when evaluating business software:

- **Bespoke vs. Productized:** Built specifically for this customer, or off-the-shelf?
- **Flexible vs. Guided:** Does it enforce a workflow, or leave structure to the user?

<SaasQuadrant client:load era="before" title="The SaaS Landscape" />

Most enterprise SaaS lives in the bottom-right: Workflow Software. Productized and guided. Shopify, Salesforce, industry-specific ERPs. These are the systems that run most businesses.

The top-right quadrant — Adaptive Systems — is what every sophisticated buyer actually wants. Software that enforces structured workflows but is built specifically for how their business operates. Historically, only the largest enterprises could afford it. Everyone else compromised.

## The Precursor: Low-Code Tools

The demand was always there. Retool and Airtable took this problem on.

At a $50M ARR manufacturing marketplace, we replaced purpose-built SaaS tools with Retool and Airtable workflows. Not because we preferred them. Because the off-the-shelf options didn't fit, and these let us build something closer to what we actually needed without a full engineering cycle.

The result was clumsy. Retool requires a developer. Airtable breaks at scale. The UX is obviously stitched together. But we got workflows that matched our operations instead of the reverse.

That's the demand signal. Companies will put up with clumsy tools to get something that fits. The question was always whether something cleaner was possible.

## AI Changes the Build Economics

The cost to move from productized to bespoke has dropped sharply. A small team can now build a guided, workflow-enforcing system tailored to a specific customer's operations at a fraction of what it cost three years ago.

This doesn't mean SaaS is going away. It means the category is fragmenting. Buyers who accepted generic tools because bespoke was unaffordable now have options. Builders who needed large engineering teams to serve them don't.

The result is hyper-verticalization: software built for smaller and smaller customer segments, with tighter structural fit to how each segment actually operates. In the limit, personalization for each customer.

<SaasQuadrant client:load era="after" title="The Shift" />

## My Test

I'm building ERPForge to test this directly. The hypothesis: an AI-assisted ERP that adapts to a specific company's operations, at a build cost that makes it viable for small and mid-sized manufacturers.

Retool and Airtable took this problem on. The question is whether AI gets the rest of the way — where the new floor on build cost lands, and whether the resulting product is structurally strong enough to support real operations or just a cleaner version of the same clumsy workaround.
AI development tools are the new leverage. They won't topple every software moat, but they change who gets to attack.

## The Original Barbarians

In 1988, KKR bought RJR Nabisco for $25 billion. They didn't know how to run a tobacco-and-food conglomerate. They didn't need to.

What made the deal possible wasn't operational expertise. It was a new class of financial instrument. Michael Milken's junk bond network gave firms like KKR access to capital structures that turned $15 million in equity into multi-billion-dollar acquisitions. The leverage ratio was absurd. The playbook was simple: find an undervalued company, load it with debt, extract value.

Most of those firms weren't better operators. Many failed. But enough succeeded to permanently change how corporate America thought about defensibility. The moat wasn't ownership anymore. It was whether you could actually run the business once you had it.

## The New Leverage

AI development tools (Lovable, Cursor, Claude, v0) are doing to software what junk bonds did to acquisitions. They're not making everyone a software engineer. They're giving people who understand business logic the ability to build without one.

That distinction matters. The bottleneck in most SaaS platforms was never the individual transaction logic. It's straightforward. The complexity is in encoding thousands of business rules, edge cases, and operational workflows into code. That required teams of engineers who often didn't fully understand the domain, translating requirements from people who did.

Now the people who understand the business logic can write the rules themselves. Not all of them. Not perfectly. But enough to get 70% of the way to a working platform in days instead of months.

And that changes the math on whether to attempt the other 30%.

## What Still Holds

Distribution. Sales teams. Network effects. Regulatory compliance. Data moats built on years of customer activity. DevOps at scale. None of these get easier because someone can prompt their way to a working prototype.

The barbarians of the 1980s still had to operate the companies they bought. Many couldn't. Building the platform is becoming the easy part. Running it, selling it, and scaling it still require everything they always did.

## The Shift

KKR didn't win every deal. They didn't need to. They changed the game by making it possible to *try*. Incumbents who had coasted on the sheer difficulty of replication suddenly had to defend on merit.

AI tools won't topple every SaaS company. But they're about to increase the number of credible attackers, lower the cost of each attempt, and expose which systems were only defensible because they were expensive to rebuild.

Phase two is the harder question: can a product consultant's workflow be codified into reusable AI skills? Discovery questions, design reviews, BOM interviews, spec generation. If yes, the next custom ERP builds faster than this one, and the one after that faster still. The skills become the product. The ERP is what they produce. ## The Problem Traditional ERPs exist because code was expensive. Vendors built lowest-common-denominator software for a business segment, then tried to configure it per customer. Big customers got the most features. Small ones got the base package or cobbled together Excel and point solutions. At MacroFab, we built manufacturing workflows in-house because MRPs were expensive and slow to implement. The cost structure forced that tradeoff. Build it yourself or settle for software that doesn't match your operations. What if the cost structure changed? ## The Approach I architected the system with ChatGPT. Talked through the design on a walk, generated a `CLAUDE.md` file and an architecture doc, then used Claude to build the full platform in a day. The interesting part isn't the ERP. It's the layer on top: Claude skills for design review, discovery question templates, documentation generation. The skills *are* the product. The ERP is proof the process works. - **`/design-review`** structured 10-section review before writing any code - **Discovery templates** 80 questions across 12 categories for BOM and product scoping - **`/write-docs`** auto-generates API reference, migration guides, and changelogs The BOM rebuild is the clearest example. I gave Claude context on typical BOM structures and manufacturing processes, gave it skills around BOM information, and had it interview me about product workflows and configurations. Then it rebuilt the data model. Four hours from kickoff to a restructured, production-ready BOM system. Work that would normally take a systems integrator weeks. ## What It Does Eight integrated modules: Products & BOM, Quotes, Orders, Inventory, Purchasing, Manufacturing, Shipping, and Invoices. The full quote-to-order-to-ship workflow runs end to end. The BOM system is the deepest module. Recursive multi-level BOMs with revision control, alternate components, CSV import with column auto-detection, and depth-first cost rollup through the full tree.
## What's Actually Hard Cloud hosting was new territory. A full day to get Railway + Cloudflare configured with containers, DNS, and security. That was the easy problem. The harder one is encoding a consultant's judgment. A good product consultant doesn't just ask questions, they know which questions unlock the right configuration, in what order, and how to translate the answer into an architecture decision. Turning that into skills Claude can run reliably requires getting explicit about knowledge that usually lives in someone's head. That's what skill authoring is actually about, and it's slower than writing code. The next milestone is automating the loop: full interview, build, and iteration without manual orchestration. That's the difference between "I can build an ERP fast" and "a product consultant with this tool can deliver a custom ERP to a manufacturer efficiently." ## What This Proves (So Far) A product leader with the right AI workflow can stand up a realistic manufacturing ERP in days. Phase one is proven. Phase two is live now: skill authoring and building the platform layer that automates the consultant workflow. The bet is that the skills and templates used to build this ERP can build the next one faster, and that the gap between "expert needed" and "anyone with domain knowledge can" keeps closing.

import BuildTimeline from '../../components/BuildTimeline.tsx'; ## The Thesis Test AI has made a new class of software viable: apps built not for a market, but for one person's exact context and workflow. The economics never worked before. A fishing log app built for how I specifically think and fish wasn't worth building until now. But the more interesting finding isn't speed. It's what building at full depth for a single user teaches you about AI-driven feature design. How do you turn raw USGS flow data into a condition summary a fisherman can act on? How do you build voice input that produces a structured log without a form? These are the same problems SaaS teams face when building personalized features at scale, just faster and lower-stakes to work through here. catch.ai is a testbed for those patterns. ## The Problem Fishing trips generate useful data. Location, conditions, what worked, what didn't. I was tracking it across four tools: handwritten notes, Google Maps pins, manually pulled USGS stream data, and ChatGPT for pattern questions. Nothing connected. I couldn't find patterns across trips, and every spot looked the same in my memory. ## The Process I brainstorm on walks, talking through product thinking with ChatGPT. That produces a guidelines file. Design and architecture decisions captured before touching any build tool. From there: ~10 prompts to set up the core structure and speech-to-text tooling. Four hours from zero to a working demo. - **Research & scoping:** ChatGPT for feature definition, API exploration, creative brainstorming - **Guidelines file:** Architecture and design decisions captured before touching Lovable - **Build:** Lovable for the full application. UI, backend, data layer. ~10 prompts to working app. - **Zero code written.** Every implementation decision was directed through prompts. ## What It Does **Voice log to AI normalization.** Talk through a trip naturally. The app transcribes and normalizes it into a structured log entry: species, location, conditions, techniques, outcome. No forms. **AI suggestions.** A fishing assistant with access to your log history. More like a knowledgeable guide than a generic chatbot. **USGS data integration** *(in progress).* Raw API responses from USGS stream gauges translated into plain-language fishing condition summaries.
## What's Actually Hard The 4-hour demo proves the thesis directionally. But the edge cases reveal where AI tooling still has friction: - **Maps integration:** Getting the UI right took more iteration than the core app logic. - **Safari microphone access:** Mobile browser permissions are a pain point that Lovable can't abstract away. - **Security:** Cloudflare configuration to prevent AI endpoint abuse required manual problem-solving outside the AI toolchain. - **USGS database:** The upstream data structure is messy. Harder to work with than expected, and not something prompts can easily fix. The pattern: core product logic is fast. Platform integrations, security, and upstream data quality are where the time goes. ## What This Proves (So Far) A product leader with AI tools can get to a working, deployed consumer app in an afternoon. But the more interesting question isn't speed to first demo. It's depth. Can you make real product decisions about external data integrations? Can you build transformation layers that interpret messy upstream data? Can you ship features like voice-to-structured-data that would normally require dedicated engineering? Early answer: yes, with caveats. The core product logic and AI features are fast. Platform integrations, security, and upstream data quality are where the time goes. The broader connection: the patterns here — turning raw external data into user value through an AI layer, designing input flows around how a person actually works — show up in SaaS product design too. catch.ai and ERPForge are testing the same thesis at different scales. One is a personal app built for a single user. The other is a custom business system built for a specific manufacturer. Both are asking how far AI-driven feature design can go when you don't have to build for the average case.
